preface.p: This set of lessons is designed to be used as pre-class or in-class activities for a flipped or other active learning class for a first semester calculus course covering limits, derivatives, and integrals.

introduction.p: Calculus is concerned with addressing problems that involve some kind of infinity. In this first activity we will work with two examples where a pattern in slopes requires us to consider infinitely many cases. The first case is typical of what traditional high school algebra courses consider. It derives from the question, "What is the slope of a single point?"

The second case is a function for which there is no formula, though we can precisely describe it. This example will be used throughout the semester to answer questions about what is possible. We are still considering the question, "What is the slope of a single point?"
We have succeeded in learning from this activity when we can make sense of the question about calculating a slope of (at) a single point.

subsection.title: Developing a Definition
subsection.p: This section is entitled discovering limits. Why is it discover rather than learn? This is designed to mimic mathematics in life. In life people typically notice a recurring trait in something (make an observation). They take time to describe the trait carefully, likely using many examples. Through this process of careful description, they construct a definition. This is to say that definitions are not printed on the universe: they are simply the result of people describing a phenomenon in a way that enables them to work with it.

In this section we will practice this process of noticing a recurring trait and constructing a definition. Because the examples below have been curated, we will end up noticing some important traits of functions that led over a couple hundred years to the modern definitions for limits.

subsection.title: Nicer Curves
subsection.p: A major theme of this course is learning properties of curves that make them nice, that is in some context it is easier to work with them. The first of these properties is a limit being defined at a point, or, even nicer, the limit being defined on an interval. Defined on an interval means that the limit is defined at every point in that interval.

In this section we are describing limits visually. We will work on a symbolic definition for use in calculations in other sections. For now we will be satisfied by being able to give visual descriptions of what functions (graphs) look like at a point or on an interval where the limit is defined.

subsection.p: In general it is not practical to prove limits directly using the definition. First, it requires already knowing what the limit should be. Second, the algebra can be quite difficult. Finally, the algebra does little to explain what it means for the limit to exist at a point.

introduction.p: Rather than guess the value of a limit and then attempt to prove it using a definition, we will use the definitions to prove some basic limit forms and prove some arithmetic properties of limits. These will allow us to evaluate limits similar to the way we would evaluate a function. The goal is to solve a problem like \lim_{x \to 5} \frac{3x^2-7}{x+3} by using the properties to break it up into known, basic forms.
We will then show then demonstrate that this method does not always work. This restriction is part of the theme that we cannot treat the infinite like the finite.

subsection.title: Basic Limits
subsection.p: Note any two sided limit implies both one sided limits. For example \lim_{x \to a^+} x = a. is also true. This implication says simply if the limit is defined from both sides, then it is certainly defined from one (either) side. Also the limit \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{x^2} = \infty is actually not a basic form, but rather a result of the previous two in the list. However, it is convenient to memorize it at this point.

Proofs of some of these basic forms are provided for three reasons. First, who would want to base their calculations or solutions or statements that are only appear to be true because we looked at insufficient examples? Truth here is means that we can arrive at this conclusion based on basic facts (think axioms and definitions) and logic.

If you object that you are more than willing to accept these as true, trusting the mathematicians to not pull a fast one on you, then note the second reason to present these proofs is that they are part of mathematics culture. For many mathematicians if there is no proof it is not mathematics. For those who think, if there is no application it is not meaningful, you should understand that these are both statements of personal values.

Finally, remember that evaluating limits is not an important task in life, that is, it is unlikely you will do much if any of this in your careers. Some of these proofs in addition to establishing truth, help us make sense of the statement. For example what does it mean that 1/x^2 becomes infinite as x approaches 0? What does infinity even mean?

subsection.title: Properties of Limits
subsection.p: Now that we know the limits of some very basic forms, we need to learn how to combine these forms to evaluate more complicated forms.

claim.p: In symbols \lim_{x \to a} [f(x)+g(x)] = \left[ \lim_{x \to a} f(x) \right] + \left[ \lim_{x \to a} g(x) \right].

proof.p: The goal is to show that \lim_{x \to a} [f(x)+g(x)] = \lim_{x \to a} f(x) + \lim_{x \to a} g(x).

Suppose \lim_{x \to a} f(x)=L_f and \lim_{x \to a} g(x)=L_g. By definition of these limits for all \epsilon/2 there exists some \delta_f > 0 and \delta_g > 0 such that |x-a| < \delta_f \text{ implies } |f(x)-L_f| < \epsilon/2 and |x-a| < \delta_g \text{ implies } |g(x)-L_g| < \epsilon/2. Thus for \delta=\min(\delta_f,\delta_g)
Thus for all \epsilon > 0 there exists a \delta=\min(\delta_f,\delta_g) > 0 such that |x-a| < \delta implies |[f(x)+g(x)]-[L_f+L_g]| < \epsilon.

When the many mathematical symbols you know began to be used, Thomas Harriot made the statement that mathematics was now covered over in a scab of symbols. As with other problems in mathematics, sometimes the difficulty in evaluating a limit is the form in which we have written it. Specifically, the notation leads to arithmetic with infinity for which sense cannot be made. Modifying that algebraic form by applying algebra, trigonometry, or other ideas enables us to recognize the value of the limit. Our interest here is not so much evaluating the limit (the number or infinity at the end), but rather recognizing how odd infinity is.

We have two goals for this section.
Learn to use four techniques for handling limits that cannot be evaluated directly using continuity.
Learn to identify the issue that informs us when to select each technique.

subsection.title: Oscillations (and more): Squeeze Theorem
subsection.p: This technique is often used to handle dampened oscillations (think functions with sine or cosine).

We know that a limit does not exist if there are bad oscillations which means the function oscillates infinitely many times in the interval considered and those oscillations do not dampen (amplitude drops to zero). If the oscillations are finite or do dampen, then the limit can exist. One way of showing that a limit with infinite, dampened oscillation exists is to show that it is squeezed (dampened) to a specific value.

statement.p: Graph \frac{-9}{x^2+3x}, \frac{-5}{x^2+3x}, \frac{2\cos(x)-7}{x^2+3x} together. See how the third expression remains between the first two as you look to the right.

Evaluate \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{2\cos(x)-7}{x^2+3x}. Note that the cosine will oscillate infinitely. This suggests using the squeeze theorem. We will start with what we know about \cos(x) and use algebra to convert that into the expression in this limit.

Look at the first step.
Why did we want a cos(x)?
Note we know the bounds by knowing cos(x): it has nothing to do with this problem.
The steps were multiply, add, divide in that order. What order is this (what other problems use this order)?
In the penultimate (second to last) step what is the expression in the middle? Why do we want that for this problem?
For the squeeze theorem to be useful, we need to know the limits on the left and right. We start with the limit on the left for no good reason.

For the limit on the right, notice that the steps will be the same except for writing -5 instead of -9. The result is still 0. Because our limit must remain below the right limit and above the left limit, and they both go to 0 the squeeze theorem tells us \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{2\cos(x)-7}{x^2+3x}=0. This means this was a well-behaved oscillation (infinite oscillations, but damped).

subsection.title: Derivatives and Tangent Slopes
subsection.p: Consider . The line through points A and B intersects the curve in at least those two points. But as A approaches B those intersections are close together. In the limit, points A and B overlap (become one point). That means the line intersects this curve at only one point. This is a common description of a tangent line. They are sometimes known as osculating curves. Osculate is Latin for barely touch (also used to mean kiss). In context the line barely touches the curve.

Another perspective on this tangent line comes from considering the direction a person travelling along the curve is facing. Suppose a person is at point A looking toward point B. As they approach B they would not be looking across the curve but just along the curve. This defines the direction of the curve. It is also the direction the person would go if they slipped (direction they are headed at that moment).

example.p: Consider the function f(x)=x^2. We will write an equation for the line tangent to f(x) at x=3. To write the equation of a line we need a point and the slope at that point.

Because of the meaning of a derivative (limit on the slopes is the tangent slope), the slope of the tangent line will be the value of derivative.
\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^2-3^2}{x-3} = \amp \lim_{x \to 3} \frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{(x-3)} = \amp \lim_{x \to 3} (x+3) = \amp 6.
The point is (3,3^2)=(3,9). Now we can write an equation for this line: \frac{y-9}{x-3}=6. Graph this line and the parabola to confirm that they are tangential (osculate at the point (3,9)).

subsection.title: The derivative as a function
subsection.p: Finally in this section consider that we can determine if the derivative is defined at every point on a curve. For many of the curves we know, they are differentiable at all points where they are defined (a list is below). This means that while a derivative is defined as a property of a point on a curve, we can expand the concept to refer to the derivative as a property of the whole function.

We define the derivative of a function f(x) to be the function, denoted f'(x), to be the function such that f'(a)=\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a} for all a where it is defined. For a function y=f(x) this is also denoted \frac{dy}{dx}=f'(x).

example.p: Consider the function f(x)=sin(x). We will write an equation for the line tangent to f(x) at x=\pi/4. To write the equation of a line we need a point and the slope at that point.

The point is \left( \frac{\pi}{4}, \sin\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) \right) = \left( \frac{\pi}{4}, 1 \right). The sloe is given by the derivative.
f'(\pi/4) = \amp \cos(\pi/4) = \amp 1 . Thus an equation of the tangent line to sine at \pi/4 is \frac{y-1}{x-\pi/4} = 1.

In pre-calculus classes equations related information like side lengths and angle measures of triangles (e.g., Pythagorean Theorem, law of cosines). subsection.title: Related Rates
subsection.p: Implicit differentiation is needed in some applications. The expression related rates will make sense after considering examples.

statement.p: Air is being pumped into a spherical balloon so that its volume increases at a rate of 100 \text{cm}^3/\text{s}. How fast is the radius of the balloon increasing when the diameter is 50cm?

solution.p: First, we need to look up a formula for the volume of a sphere. It is V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3. Next note that we are told the change in volume is 100. Change in volume means we know the derivative of V with respect to time. We also note that time is not an explicit variable (i.e., there is no variable t). Thus to use this formula we need to differentiate the it. V^\prime=\frac{4}{3}\pi 3r^2 r^\prime. Note we need the r^\prime at the end because the radius is also a function of time; thus we use implicit differentiation. Finally we can plug in the values we were given. Note r=25 cm because the diameter is 50 cm.

subsection.p: Notice that in the rate of change of the radius is related to the rate of change of the volume. This is the origin of the name related rates.

The process we followed is below.
In an application notice rates of change (derivatives).
Develop a model or (as necessary) look up a formula for the application.
Differentiate the model.
Insert given values including calculating some as necessary.

The most common mistake in working on related rates is to insert numbers too early. We must differentiate before inserting numbers. If we insert numbers (constants) early, then the derivative (change) will be zero. This will not match the circumstance unless that parameter never changes (e.g., a fixed length like a height of a wall).

One of the uses of derivatives is to identify traits of functions such as highest and lowest points. These are optimizations in many applications (i.e., find the lowest cost or maximum profit).

subsection.title: Absolute Extrema
subsection.p: First, we will think about traits of highest and lowest points on specified sections of curves (functions over a limited domain).

An absolute maximum is the highest point of a function/curve on a specified interval. An absolute minimum is the lowest point of a function/curve on a specified interval. Collectively maxima and minima are known as extrema.

statement.p: A value c \in [a,b] is an absolute maximum of a function f over the interval [a,b] if and only if f(c) \ge f(x) for all x \in [a,b].
A value c \in [a,b] is an absolute minimum of a function f over the interval [a,b] if and only if f(c) \le f(x) for all x \in [a,b].

example.title: Graphing a Function Using Derivatives
example.p: We can represent functions by graphing them. However, there is a question about which points should be plotted to understand the function. If we plot too few or in the wrong places, we will miss important details. The question about which points we need to plot is answered in part by knowing the connection between first derivative and increasing and decreasing segments and the connection between second derivative and concave up and down.
We will consider the function g(y)=\frac{y^2-4y}{y+2}.

First we determine where the function is defined (the domain). We know these are places where the derivatives will also be undefined, so changes can take place across these. We will also need limits approaching these values.
For a rational function undefined points will occur solely where the denominator is zero.

For this function the undefined points occur where
y+2 = \amp 0. y = \amp -2.
So the domain is (-\infty,-2) \cup (-2,\infty).
Second we determine where the function might change between increasing and decreasing. This occurs where the first derivative is 0 or undefined (critical values).
Third we determine where the function changes between concave up and down. This happens where the second derivative is 0 or undefined.
Now that we know where to look we can test where the function is increasing/decreasing and concave up/down by testing between the values y=-2, 2-2\sqrt{3}, 2+2\sqrt{3}. These are shown in .

For example at x=-1.5 g^\prime(-1.5)=-47. Because it is negative we know the curve is decreasing on this interval. We do not need that it is -47 so we record only -. g''(-1.5)=192. Because it is positive the curve is concave up on this interval.

Finally we can use this information to graph g(y). First plot the points calculated. Next consider the interval [-3,-2). The curve is decreasing (g^\prime(y) \lt 0) concave down (g''(y) \lt 0). This looks like the top right in . To determine whether the function has a hole or a jump at y=2 we need the following limits.
\lim_{y \to -2^-} g(y) = \amp \lim_{y \to -2^-} \frac{y^2-4y}{y+2} = \amp \left( \lim_{y \to -2^-} y^2-4y \right) \left( \lim_{y \to -2^-} \frac{1}{y+2} \right) = \amp \left( \lim_{y \to -2^-} y^2-4y \right) \left( \lim_{u \to 0^-} \frac{1}{u} \right) = \amp
The left expression is continuous, so we can evaluate it. The right limit we know is -\infty. Thus this limit is negative infinity.

We move to the next interval (-2,2-2\sqrt{3}). This is decreasing (g^\prime(y) \lt 0) concave up (g''(y) \gt 0). This looks like the bottom left in . To finish determining what happens at y=-2 we need the limit from the right.
\lim_{y \to -2^+} g(y) = \amp \lim_{y \to -2^+} \frac{y^2-4y}{y+2} = \amp \left( \lim_{y \to -2^+} y^2-4y \right) \left( \lim_{y \to -2^+} \frac{1}{y+2} \right) = \amp \left( \lim_{y \to -2^+} y^2-4y \right) \left( \lim_{u \to 0^+} \frac{1}{u} \right) = \amp
This limit is positive infinity. This means g(y) has an infinite jump at y=-2.
The next interval is (-2,2+2\sqrt{3}) which is also decreasing concave up. Even though the first derivative was zero, nothing changed here.
Moving to the next interval which is (2+2\sqrt{3},6). This is increasing (g^prime(y) \gt 0) concave up (g''(y) \gt 0). This looks like the bottom right in .

The last two segments are (-\infty,-3) and (6,\infty). To know where these go we need to following limits.
\lim_{y \to -\infty} g(y) = \amp \lim_{y \to -\infty} \frac{y^2-4y}{y+2} = \amp \text{ handle } \infty/\infty \lim_{y \to -\infty} \frac{\frac{1}{y}(y^2-4y)}{\frac{1}{y}(y+2)} = \amp \lim_{y \to -\infty} \frac{y-4}{1+\frac{2}{y}} = \amp -\infty. \lim_{y \to -\infty} g(y) = \amp \lim_{y \to \infty} \frac{y^2-4y}{y+2} = \amp \text{ handle } \infty/\infty \lim_{y \to \infty} \frac{\frac{1}{y}(y^2-4y)}{\frac{1}{y}(y+2)} = \amp \lim_{y \to \infty} \frac{y-4}{1+\frac{2}{y}} = \amp \infty.
The first limit (to the left) is for a concave down segment. The second (to the right) is concave up.
Finally this information can be used to graph.

subsection.title: Interpreting Functions and Derivatives in Context
subsection.p: While graphing produces nifty images from functions, the derivatives can also be used to interpret functions in context.

example.title: Interpreting Distance
example.p: Consider the function s(t) which represents the distance of a person from home at a time given in minutes.
If s'(t) \gt 0 for t \in [0,5], then the person's distance from home is increasing. Phrased simply the person is going away from home for those five minutes.
If s''(t) \lt 0 and s'(t) \gt 0 for t \in [10,15], then the person is getting farther away from home (1st derivative) but slowing down (2nd derivative).
If s'(t)=0 for t \in [20,25] then the person is not moving for those five minutes (might be practicing social distancing).
If s''(t) \lt 0 and s'(t) \lt 0 for t \in [30,35], the person is returning home and increasing speed toward home. Perhaps the person is going to celebrate the great grade on a calculus exam.

example.title: Interpreting Product Demand
example.p: Consider the function d(t) which represents the number of widgets sold on day t.
If d'(t) \gt 0 for t \in [0,5], then the number of widgets sold per day is increasing. Demand is increasing.
If d''(t) \lt 0 and d'(t) \gt 0 for t \in [10,15], then the number of widgets sold each day is increasing (1st derivative), but each day the increase is smaller (2nd derivative).
If d'(t)=0 for t \in [20,25] then the number of widgets being sold is not changing. Note this does not mean none are sold: it could be that 20 are sold each day because that is no change in demand.
If d''(t) \lt 0 and d'(t) \lt 0 for t \in [30,35], the number of widgets sold each day is decreasing greater each day. I hope you sold your stock in this company.

subsection.title: Statement of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

statement.p:
For a function f that is continuous on an interval [a,b]
Part 1
Let F(x) = \int_a^x f(t) \; dt for x \in [a,b] then F(x) is differentiable and F^\prime(x) = f(x).
Part 2
For any function G(x) that is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b) such that G^\prime(x) = f(x) then \int_a^b f(x) \; dx = G(b)-G(a)

example.p:
We want to calculate \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos\theta \; d\theta According to the FTC Part 2 we can do this if we know a function G(\theta) such that G^\prime(\theta)=\cos\theta. Thankfully, we know that the derivative of G(\theta)=\sin\theta is \cos\theta. Thus by the FTC
\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos\theta \; d\theta & = \sin(\pi/2)-\sin(0) & = 1 - 0 & = 1

For convenience we have a notation to help us break up the steps. Below is the same problem as above using the evaluation notation.
\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos\theta \; d\theta & = \left. \sin(\theta) \right|_0^{\pi/2} & = \sin(\pi/2)-\sin(0) & = 1 - 0 & = 1

We want to calculate \int_1^5 3x^2 \; dx According to the FTC Part 2 we can do this if we know a function G(x) such that G^\prime(x)=3x^2. Thankfully, we know that the derivative of G(x)=x^3 is 3x^2. Thus by the FTC
\int_1^5 3x^2 \; dx & = \left. x^3 \right|_1^5 & = 5^3-1^3 & = 125 - 1 & = 124

subsection.title: Function Inverses

statement.p: A mapping f from a set A called the domain to a set B called the codomain is a function if and only if for each a \in A there exists exactly one b \in B such that f(a)=b.

subsection.p: Note that the definition depends on how many elements are paired. Consider |x|+|y|=1. If x=3/4, note that both y=1/4 and y=-1/4 work. Thus y is not a function of x because there are two outputs. This is a nice mapping which you can graph. Try it!

statement.p: The inverse mapping of a mapping f from domain A to codomain B is the mapping f^{-1} from the domain B to the codomain A such that if f(a)=b then f^{-1}(b)=a.

subsection.p: If the inverse mapping of a function is also a function, then it is called the inverse function. For example, r(\theta)=\sin(\theta) is a function, but its inverse is not a function, because both r^{-1}(0)=0 and r^{-1}(\pi)=0.

statement.p: A function is one-to-one if and only if f(a)=f(b) implies a=b.

subsection.p: Note this definition is expressed backwards. It means the function is not the same at any two places. For example r(\theta)=\sin(\theta) is not one-to-one because r(0)=r(\pi) but 0 \ne \pi, that is r(\theta) has the same value at two different places.

subsection.p: The following example begins with an integrand that looks similar to the derivative of inverse sine, but has coefficients other than one. Algebra enables us to transform it into the desired form. \int \frac{5}{\sqrt{16-32x^2}} dx = \amp \int \frac{5}{\sqrt{16(1-2x^2)}} dx = \amp \int \frac{5}{4\sqrt{1-2x^2}} dx = \amp \frac{5}{4} \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2x^2}} dx u^2 = \amp 2x^2 u = \amp \sqrt{2}x du = \amp \sqrt{2} dx = \amp \frac{5}{4\sqrt{2}} \int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{1-2x^2}} dx = \amp \frac{5}{4\sqrt{2}} \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}} du = \amp \frac{5}{4\sqrt{2}} \arcsin u + C = \amp \frac{5}{4\sqrt{2}} \arcsin(\sqrt{2}x) + C.

introduction.p: A lost hiker is holding a signal mirror 5 ft above the ground and pointing it at a helicopter that is flying toward him at 2000 ft AGL at 10 mph.

statement.p: What is the rate at which the angle of the mirror is changing when the helicopter is 1000 ft away from the hiker?

solution.p: First we note that this situation is a right triangle with the base shrinking. The height of the triangle is 2000-5=1995 ft. Because the height is in feet we convert the speed to feet per second. \frac{10 \text{ mi}}{\text{hr}} \cdot \frac{5280 \text{ ft}}{3600 \mbox{ s}} \approx \frac{14.7 \text{ ft}}{\text{s}}.

The model for distances is \tan\theta = \frac{1995}{b}. To calculate the rate at which the mirror is tipped (\theta^\prime) we differentiate the model. (\sec^2\theta) \theta^\prime = -\frac{1995}{b^2}b^\prime. At the time about which we are asked, we know that b=1000. We must calculate \theta at this moment. We know that \tan\theta = \frac{1995}{1000} so \theta \approx 1.106. Thus \theta^\prime = -\frac{1995}{1000^2 \cdot \sec^2(1.106)}14.7 \approx 0.0131453322.
